pool.prompt: Which fiber optic cable type is required for installation in an air-handling plenum?
choices: OFNR — passes the riser vertical flame test
OFNG — unlisted general use
OFNP — passes UL 910 / NFPA 262 flame and smoke test
Any cable rated OSP with UV-stabilized HDPE jacket
pool.explanation: OFNP (Optical Fiber Nonconductive Plenum) is required in air-handling plenums, passing UL 910 / NFPA 262 for low flame spread and low smoke density. OFNR can be used in riser shafts but NOT in plenums.

pool.prompt: An unlisted outdoor OSP cable enters a commercial building at grade level. The termination panel is 35 ft from the building entry. What is required?
choices: Transition to OFNP immediately at the building entry
No additional action — 35 ft is under the 50 ft unlisted-entry limit in NEC Section 770.48(A)
Transition to OFNR at the 25 ft mark
The cable cannot enter a building at all without a transition
pool.explanation: 35 ft is within the 50 ft unlisted entry allowance under NEC Section 770.48(A). The 50-ft limit applies to the total run of unlisted cable inside the building, measured from the point of entrance, and can be extended further with RMC/IMC conduit.
pool.fieldNote: Always confirm with the local AHJ — some jurisdictions require indoor fire-rated cable for any interior run regardless of the 50 ft federal code provision.

pool.prompt: What does the carbon black content (typically 2-3%) in HDPE OSP jacket material provide?
choices: Increased tensile strength for aerial spans
UV resistance — it absorbs UV radiation and prevents oxidative photodegradation that would otherwise make the jacket brittle within a few years
Fire resistance equivalent to LSZH jackets
Improved splice loss performance
pool.explanation: Carbon black is added specifically to absorb UV radiation and prevent oxidative photodegradation. Without it, the HDPE jacket would become brittle and crack within a few years of sun exposure — this is why nearly all outdoor OSP cable jackets are black.

pool.prompt: Which cable type can legally substitute for OFNR cable in a building riser shaft?
choices: OFNG (unlisted general-use)
Standard OSP with HDPE jacket
OFNP (plenum-rated)
No cable can substitute — only OFNR is permitted in riser shafts
pool.explanation: OFNP, being rated for the more demanding plenum environment (stricter flame/smoke requirements), can substitute for OFNR in a riser shaft — a higher-rated cable can always fill a lower-rated application's role, but not vice versa.

pool.prompt: Why can't an OFNR-rated cable be substituted for OFNP in a plenum space?
choices: OFNR and OFNP are functionally identical, so substitution is always fine

OFNR is rated to the less stringent riser vertical-flame-spread test, not the plenum-specific low-smoke/flame test (UL 910 / NFPA 262) that a plenum space requires — the rating hierarchy only allows substituting UP, not down
OFNR cable is physically incompatible with plenum spaces due to size
OFNP is always cheaper than OFNR, so there's no reason to substitute downward anyway
pool.explanation: Fire/smoke rating hierarchy runs one direction: a higher-rated cable (OFNP) can be used where a lower rating (OFNR) is specified, but not the reverse. OFNR has not been tested to the more stringent plenum-specific standard, so it cannot legally substitute for OFNP.

pool.prompt: An unlisted OSP cable needs to run 80 ft inside a building from its point of entrance — beyond the standard 50 ft allowance. What is the correct way to legally extend this?
choices: It cannot be done; the cable must be entirely replaced with a listed indoor cable
Enclose the cable in RMC (rigid metal conduit) or IMC (intermediate metal conduit) — the 50-ft measurement restarts from where the cable exits the conduit
Simply document an exception and proceed with the unlisted cable at 80 ft
Splice to a shorter listed cable segment only for the final 30 ft
pool.explanation: NEC allows extending the effective point of entrance by continuously enclosing the unlisted cable in RMC or IMC conduit. The 50-ft unlisted-cable allowance then measures from where the cable emerges from that conduit, not from the original building entry point.

pool.prompt: Why does NEC Article 770 distinguish 'plenum,' 'riser,' and general unlisted-cable ratings rather than using one universal indoor fiber cable spec?
choices: The distinction is purely a marketing device with no fire-safety basis

Different indoor spaces present different fire/smoke propagation risks — plenums circulate air throughout a building (making smoke/flame spread especially dangerous), while risers are vertical shafts with their own but different vertical fire-spread risk — each demands a matched cable rating
Plenum and riser cable are electrically different and cannot be interchanged for signal-quality reasons
The distinction only applies to copper cable, not fiber
pool.explanation: Plenum spaces are part of the building's air-handling system, so a fire there can spread smoke and flame throughout the building via ductwork — hence the strictest test (UL 910/NFPA 262). Riser shafts pose a different but still serious vertical fire-spread risk, hence a distinct riser test. Matching cable rating to actual fire-risk profile is the point of the distinction.

pool.prompt: Match each fiber cable fire rating to its typical installation environment.

items.label: Up to 50 ft inside a building from point of entrance

pool.explanation: OFNP is required in plenum spaces (strictest fire/smoke test). OFNR is required in vertical riser shafts. Unlisted OSP cable is permitted for a limited run (50 ft, extendable via conduit) from the building's point of entrance under NEC 770.48(A).
